Someone Bought This Ford Thunderbird in 2002 and Parked It. 24 Years Later, It Has 29 Miles
29 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
To make a long story short, this 2002 Ford Thunderbird was driven off the showroom floor, parked in a climate-controlled garage, and never touched again. Now, the car is out in broad daylight, sitting at the dealership and ready to find another owner.
Just 29.3 miles or 47.15 kilometers. This is how far this 2002 Ford Thunderbird has traveled since it rolled off the production line. It wasn’t even taken out for maintenance because at that sort of mileage, it hasn't required any. Everything is original on the car, including the tires. So whoever buys this Thunderbird will have to change them ASAP if they are planning to drive it.
The car is finished in black with a matching removable hardtop and a black soft top over an interior with seats wrapped in black leather upholstery, and rides on 17-inch chrome wheels. Dual-zone automatic climate control and an in-dash CD changer are also on board.
The list of factory equipment is quite short because there is no sign of the window sticker, and the dealer can't figure out on its own everything the car came with. We can safely assume that the owner who sold it to the selling dealer back in August also had trouble remembering. There is no backstory and no plot twist on this car, even though low-mileage models always have a story to tell.
Photo: Cars and Bids What we do know is that there is a 3.9-liter Jaguar-derived V8 engine under the hood. It makes 252 horsepower (256 metric horsepower) and 267 pound-feet (362 Newton meters) of torque. That is enough for a run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.8 seconds on its way to a top speed of 130 mph (209 kph).
A 5R55N five-speed automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels. Ford never offered a manual transmission with the 11th generation of the Thunderbird, even though the automaker was well aware that it would have brought out the car's sportier side. It did, however, offer the 55R55S with manual gear-selection controls.
Built on a shortened rear-wheel-drive platform shared with the Lincoln LS and Jaguar S-Type, it was anything but a sports car. It was actually more of a smooth operator, designed and engineered to prioritize cruising and comfort over sharp handling.
When Ford revived the Thunderbird for 2002, after a five-year hiatus, initial demand was high enough that dealers marked them up and collectors stashed them away, expecting rapid appreciation. The Ford Thunderbird hit the market with a starting MSRP of $35,495, destination charges included, for the base Deluxe convertible and climbed to $41,995 for the limited-run Neiman Marcus Edition.
Photo: Cars and Bids But because initial demand far exceeded supply across the 2001 and 2002 production years, many Ford dealers charged $5,000 to $15,000 over MSRP, pushing real-world transaction prices past $50,000. Such numbers pushed it into the same segment as the BMW Z3 Roadster, Chrysler Prowler, Mercedes-Benz SLK , and Chevrolet Corvette Convertible.
This is what probably convinced collectors to buy them and park them, hoping to cash in one day. That is exactly why a very low-mileage example hits the market every once in a while. Ford built 31,368 Thunderbirds for the 2002 model year. That single year accounted for roughly 46% of the entire 2002 - 2005 eleventh-generation production run of 68,098 cars total.
However, some owners must have waited far too long to sell. On the collector car market, a 2002 Ford Thunderbird typically sells for $12,000 to $18,000 in clean, driver-grade condition, while ultra-low-mileage, time-capsule examples, such as this one, reach $26,000 to $35,000. So nobody’s getting rich selling nowadays.
With four days to go, the highest bid reached $17,250. There is still time. The future owner will get a car with a clean Carfax report with no accidents or mileage discrepancies (who would’ve thought?). They will also go home with a key and a fob, the hardtop rack, and the factory cover. No window sticker is available and, of course, there are zero service records for the car that never left the garage.
Photo: Cars and Bids From the moment this 2002 Ford Thunderbird goes home with someone else, the future owner has two options. They can park it in another climate-controlled garage and wait for the moment the collector car market is kinder to the model, and they will be able to fetch more than they paid for it.
Or they can just drive it until its wheels fall off, even though the car’s value would instantly drop. On roads where everybody drives pickup trucks and SUVs, this would really be a showstopper. It has stayed parked and hidden long enough.
This may look like the lowest-mileage Thunderbird on the face of the earth, but it is not. Another time capsule 2002 model, finished in Evening Black, surfaced back in 2026 with just 15 delivery miles (24.1 kilometers), beating the 29-mile car by 14 miles (22.5 kilometers).
